transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you. Well, it's... it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main thing that brings me in today is that I just keep getting up when I am really, absolutely supposed to stay put. 

I'm a private investigator, you see—mostly corporate fraud, some domestic cases, missing assets, things like that—so I do a lot of initial intake meetings. And lately, well, I'll have a client sitting right across my desk, right in the middle of explaining something highly sensitive, and I just can't stay in my chair. I'll pop up to adjust the window shade, or pace behind my desk, or go grab a file I don't even need yet. 

And it's not just at work, either! I do some tutoring on the side—high school kids, mostly, since I got my bachelor's degree years ago and I like to keep my hand in the academic side of things—and I'm constantly out of my seat there, too. The poor kids are trying to focus on their worksheets and I'm wandering around the kitchen island. Even at my book club! We meet every other Thursday, and last week we were talking about this really thick historical fiction novel, and I must have gotten up from the host's couch five or six times while other people were trying to speak. 

People are really starting to notice, you know? My clients, my friends, the parents of the kids I tutor... they give me these looks. It's becoming incredibly obvious to everyone that I just cannot sit and listen. I mean, I *want* to listen, I'm very invested in what they're saying, but my body just decides it's time to stand up. So, that's why I'm here. I really need to figure out why I can't just stay planted in a chair.
Can you describe how you feel while you're getting up during these situations? Do you feel restless or as though you can't sit still, or does it feel more like an impulse you can't control?

Well, it's... it's a bit of both, honestly, but maybe more of the restless feeling? It’s hard to put into exact words. It’s like... okay, so picture this: I’m sitting there, right? Let's say I'm with a client, and they're going over some really dense financial records. And I am trying to focus on the numbers, but then there's this... this hum in my legs. It starts low, almost like a vibration, and then it just builds and builds. It’s not necessarily that I’m thinking, "Oh, I must stand up right this second," it’s more that sitting still starts to feel physically uncomfortable. Like my skin is too tight, or my muscles are just itching to move. 

And it’s so frustrating because I’ll try to fight it. I’ll cross my legs, then uncross them, then tuck one foot under me, then tap my pen, but the feeling just doesn't go away. It just gets louder, if that makes sense? Like a pressure gauge that's in the red. And eventually, standing up is the only way to release that pressure. So I pop up. And the second I'm on my feet, there's this wave of relief. But of course, by then I've interrupted the client, or distracted the kid I'm tutoring, or annoyed my book club. 

It’s just... it’s exhausting, really. Because I’m constantly monitoring it. I’m sitting there thinking, "Okay, you’ve been sitting for ten minutes, just make it to fifteen. Just hold on." But the restlessness always wins. It’s like trying to hold a beach ball underwater. Eventually, it’s going to pop up, and you can't really control exactly when or how it happens. So, yeah, it's definitely a restless, uncomfortable feeling that just forces me out of the chair, whether I want to get up or not.
Does this restlessness and need to move happen in other situations as well, like when you're watching a movie, in a meeting, or riding in a car?

Oh, absolutely. Movies, cars, you name it. If I'm in the passenger seat of a car for more than twenty minutes, I'm adjusting the air vents, I'm changing the radio, I'm pulling at my seatbelt. But where it really, really gets me—and this is almost as frustrating as the meetings I was just telling you about—is when I have to do the actual solo desk work. 

Because being a private investigator isn't all glamorous stakeouts and tailing people, you know? A huge chunk of it is just sitting at a computer. And when I'm stuck at the computer, combing through endless digital records—I'm talking bank statements, phone logs, hundreds of pages of corporate emails for these fraud cases—I just cannot stay still. Even if I somehow manage to force my actual rear end to stay in the chair, my body is just doing a million other things to compensate. 

My foot will be bouncing under the desk like a jackhammer. I usually don't even realize I'm doing it until the whole desk starts vibrating and my computer monitor is physically shaking. And my hands! If I have a pen nearby, I am clicking it incessantly. Click, click, click. I actually rented a shared office space for a few months a couple of years ago, and my officemate practically threatened to throw all my pens out the second-story window because the constant clicking was driving him completely mad. I didn't blame him, honestly, but I didn't even know I was doing it until he yelled! 

And on top of the bouncing and the clicking, I'm constantly shifting my weight. I'll cross one leg, then the other, then tuck a foot up, lean forward, lean back. I shift around so much that I actually lose my place in what I'm reading. I'll be halfway down a page of a crucial, incredibly dry financial affidavit, I'll shift my hips and adjust my shoulders because I just can't take the stillness anymore, and suddenly I have no idea which line I was just looking at. Then I have to scan the whole page to find my spot, or start the entire paragraph over. It's incredibly inefficient. It just makes the computer work take twice as long as it should, which of course just means I have to sit there even longer, which makes the bouncing and the clicking and the shifting even worse! It's this awful, exhausting cycle, really, and it just makes me dread doing the research part of my job.
Can you tell me if you also have trouble staying focused or tend to get easily distracted, especially when you're trying to do tasks that require sustained mental effort?

Actually, no, not really. It’s funny you ask that, because people always seem to assume that if you can’t sit still, your mind must be a million miles away, but for me, that’s just not the case at all. My focus is actually... well, I’d say it’s pretty razor-sharp. When I’m looking into a case, like this one I had last month involving a local contractor who was supposedly funneling materials to his brother-in-law’s shell company—fascinating stuff, honestly, tracing the invoices back through three different LLCs—I was completely dialed in mentally. I didn’t lose my train of thought, I wasn't daydreaming, I wasn’t getting distracted by birds outside the window or anything like that. 

My brain knows exactly what it’s supposed to be doing. I can hold all the pieces of the puzzle in my head perfectly well. It’s just... like I was saying before, it’s the physical part that betrays me. I’ll be intensely focused on connecting a bank transfer from a few years ago to a fake vendor, completely absorbed in the logic of it, but my leg is bouncing so hard the monitor is shaking, or I have to stand up and pace the room just to keep doing the mental math. 

So, no, I don’t really have trouble staying focused mentally. If anything, I'm incredibly invested in the work, which makes it all the more aggravating that my body insists on moving around while my brain is trying to solve a puzzle. I mean, I can read a massive, complex legal brief and understand every single word, I just might have to do it while walking laps around my kitchen island, if that makes sense? So the sustained mental effort isn't the problem at all, I'm totally fine there, it's really just the sitting still part that I can't manage.
Do you ever feel this same restlessness or need to move even when you're not sitting, like when you're standing in line, waiting for something, or trying to relax on the couch?

Relaxing on the couch? Honestly, I don't think I've actually relaxed on a couch in a decade. But yes, to answer your question, it is exactly the same feeling when I'm not sitting at a desk. It’s like... well, take my days off, for example. Even on days when I don't have any active field work—no stakeouts, no client meetings, nothing officially on the calendar—I just can't turn it off. I have a really, really hard time just being off duty. 

I'll tell myself, "Okay, today is a rest day, just sit down and watch a movie or read a book for pleasure." But within five minutes, I'm up. I'll start unpacking boxes that have been sitting in my spare room for months, and then halfway through that, I'll suddenly decide I need to reorganize my old case files, and I'll spend two hours alphabetizing and cross-referencing them for absolutely no practical reason. And then I'm out the door, running errands at top speed, going to the dry cleaners, the post office, the grocery store, just darting around town like I'm chasing a hot lead on a massive case. It's the exact same energy, the exact same drive, just applied to my day off. 

And you mentioned standing in line—oh, it's agonizing. If I'm stuck in line at the grocery store during those errands, I am shifting from foot to foot, I'm constantly checking my phone, I'm looking around to see if another register is opening, I'm reorganizing my wallet... I just can't just stand there and wait. It’s like my motor is always running, just constantly idling high. So I just keep moving, keep doing things, keep finding projects around the house, because the second I try to just stop and be still on that couch, that uncomfortable, restless pressure builds right back up and forces me back on my feet.
Do you ever experience feelings of worry, nervousness, or tension along with this restlessness?

Worry? Nervousness? No, actually. Not in the slightest. It’s funny you ask that, though, because people always make that assumption. My sister, for instance, she’ll see me pacing around her kitchen island when I go over for coffee, and she’ll say, "What's wrong? Why are you so anxious?" And I always have to explain to her that I’m not anxious at all. 

My mind isn't spinning with worries, you know? I’m not sitting there fretting about whether a surveillance job is going to go south, or if a client is going to be unhappy with my findings, or stressing over my taxes or anything like that. My brain is actually completely calm in that regard. I mean, in my line of work, you kind of have to have nerves of steel anyway. If I'm sitting in my car outside a subject's house at two in the morning, I can't afford to be a nervous wreck. 

So it's completely disconnected from my emotional state. I could be having the absolute best day, totally confident about how a case is coming together, not a single care in the world, and my body will still act like it needs to run a marathon. Like, just last Tuesday, I was doing a totally routine background check—zero stakes, incredibly straightforward, I wasn't nervous about it even a fraction of a percent—and I still had to stand up and do laps around my living room just to burn off that physical buzz while I was on hold with the county clerk. 

It’s a purely physical sensation. It’s not tension like, "Oh no, what’s going to happen?" It’s tension like... like a coiled spring that just desperately needs to release kinetic energy. It’s a physical impatience, not an emotional one. So, no, I don't feel worried or scared or nervous. I'm actually a very emotionally grounded person, I just... I just have a body that refuses to stay in park. People see the bouncing foot or the pacing and they immediately think I'm having some kind of nervous crisis, but honestly, I'm just trying to burn off the battery power so I can get through the day!
